interview_metadata.name: Qiao Le
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Okay, wow, that's a huge one. Um, so I'm Qiao Neng Le, but everybody just calls me Qiao or sometimes Le-Le if they're being annoying. I was born in Ellensburg, Washington, eighteen years ago, and my parents came over from mainland China — my mom's from Hangzhou, my dad's from Chengdu — before I was born. They met here actually, weirdly, at a Chinese student association thing at Central Washington University, which is funny because that's where I'm taking community college classes now, kind of. Growing up was very, like, two-world-y. At home it was Mandarin, dumplings on Sunday, Lunar New Year with red envelopes and the whole thing, and my mom drilling me on math worksheets at the kitchen table. Then I'd go to school and be the only Asian kid in my class basically until middle school, and everybody would ask me if I ate dog, which, like, no. School was fine, I was a B+ student because I'd rather be on yearbook or in choir than studying. I did the photography club thing in tenth grade and that's when I got really into taking pictures of people. I graduated from Ellensburg High in 2025, and instead of going off to a four-year I'm doing the running-start-into-associates route at CWU, which I just finished this spring, an associate's in communications. My parents were a little disappointed I didn't get into UW for fall, but I'm reapplying for next year for their comm program. Big things in my life — um, my grandma in China passed away when I was twelve and I couldn't go to the funeral, that was hard. And my best friend Maya moved to Seattle last year and that was kind of a heartbreak in a friend way. Other than that, honestly, my life is pretty chill — hiking, hanging out, festivals, trying to figure out what I want to do.

follow_ups.question: You mentioned photography club in tenth grade — what kicked that off for you?
follow_ups.response: Honestly? I needed an elective and choir was full. But then Mr. Hendricks, the teacher, lent me this old Nikon D3200 for a weekend, and I took it to the rodeo — Ellensburg Rodeo is huge here, it's like Labor Day weekend, everybody goes — and I came back with like eight hundred photos of cowboys and kids eating funnel cake, and I was hooked. I bought my own DSLR with babysitting money, a Canon Rebel, which I still use.

follow_ups.question: What was the heartbreak with Maya moving like?
follow_ups.response: Ugh, I cried for like three days. We'd been best friends since fifth grade, we did everything together, and she got into UW for nursing and just — went. We still text every day and I go up to Seattle to see her like once a month, but it's not the same as her being three blocks away. She used to come over and we'd make dumplings with my mom on Sundays.

follow_ups.question: Are you living at home right now while you finish school?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, with my parents and my little brother Andy. He's fourteen. It's free rent and my mom's cooking, so I'm not in any rush to move out, but eventually I want to live in Seattle or maybe Portland.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yeah, definitely. So my senior year of high school, I had this thing where my parents really wanted me to apply pre-med or pre-nursing — my mom is a nurse, she works at Kittitas Valley Healthcare — and I was looking at the whole UW Bothell biology track. And at the same time, I'd been doing the social media for the Ellensburg Lunar New Year Festival, kind of as a volunteer thing, and the woman running it, Linda Tang, told me I had a real eye for it and she'd write me a recommendation if I wanted to apply for a marketing or comm program instead. I had this huge fight with my mom in like January 2025 — we were yelling in the kitchen — and I told her I wasn't going to do nursing, I was going to do communications. And I cried, she cried, my dad just made tea. But eventually they came around, partly because my GPA wasn't great for pre-med anyway. So I ended up doing the associate's first to save money and prove I could stick with it, and now I'm reapplying to UW for the comm school. That moment of saying it out loud — 'I'm not going to be a nurse' — that was the crossroads.

follow_ups.question: What did Linda see in your work that made her say that?
follow_ups.response: She said I had a knack for catching people in the middle of doing something — like a kid laughing with their mouth full of dumpling, or an auntie mid-dance. Not posed shots. And she liked that I could write the captions in English and Mandarin both, which a lot of the older folks at the festival appreciated.

follow_ups.question: Did your relationship with your mom recover from that fight?
follow_ups.response: Oh yeah, we're good now. She actually came to a festival last fall and saw all the flyers I'd made and was kind of proud, I think. She still mentions nursing like once a month — 'You know, you could still go back' — but it's a joke now, mostly.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. Like, I had to actually sit down and decide. The 'just happened' part was Linda offering the rec letter, but the saying-no-to-nursing thing was a real, scary decision I had to make on purpose.

follow_ups.question: What made you brave enough to make it?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, my friend Maya. She told me I'd be miserable doing IVs my whole life and I should just be honest with my parents now instead of dragging it out.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: I mean, my high school counselor was kind of useless, no offense. She just told me to apply to a bunch of schools and didn't really listen to what I actually wanted. If there'd been like an Asian-American mentorship thing or a comm-school outreach program in Kittitas County, that would've helped a lot. Linda kind of became that for me by accident.

follow_ups.question: Is there anything like that now for younger kids in your area?
follow_ups.response: Not really. That's actually part of why I want to do community event work — to make stuff like that exist.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: No partner, no kids, no thank you not yet. Um, family — my mom, Wei, she's the rock, she's a registered nurse and basically runs our house. My dad, Jianhua, he goes by John at work, he's an engineer at the Bonneville Power Administration substation, very quiet, very dad-jokes. Then there's Andy, my little brother, he's fourteen, he's a gremlin but I love him, he plays Valorant nonstop. We also have my grandma on my dad's side — we call her Nai Nai — who lives with us about six months out of the year and flies back to Chengdu for the rest. She's eighty-two and she makes the best dan dan noodles on the planet. My mom's parents are still in Hangzhou and we FaceTime them every Sunday at like 7 PM our time, which is Monday morning for them. I have one aunt in Vancouver, BC, my dad's sister Auntie Mei, and we drive up to see her like four times a year. That's basically the whole family. Oh, and our dog, Mochi, she's a corgi mix and she counts.

follow_ups.question: What's Sunday FaceTime with your grandparents like?
follow_ups.response: Chaotic. My grandpa is half deaf so we're all yelling into the iPad, and my grandma asks me if I have a boyfriend yet every single week, and I say no, and she sighs. Then my mom makes us speak Mandarin only and I get tongue-tied because my Mandarin is okay but not great. It takes like forty-five minutes and there's always a moment where my mom cries a little.

follow_ups.question: What's it like having Nai Nai in the house half the year?
follow_ups.response: It's actually really nice? She watches her Chinese soap operas in the living room super loud, and she teaches me cooking stuff, and she's the only one who doesn't bug me about cleaning my room because she just kind of cleans it for me. I feel guilty about that.

follow_ups.question: What does Andy think of you?
follow_ups.response: He thinks I'm uncool but he asks me for advice on girls, so. I'd say we're close in a sibling way. We watch K-dramas together sometimes when nobody's around to make fun of him for it.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have a cousin, Kevin, he's Auntie Mei's son in Vancouver, he's twenty-three and we're pretty close — he taught me how to use Photoshop. Other than that, no, that's the whole crew.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Kevin?
follow_ups.response: Maybe every two months. We text on Discord more than we see each other in person.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yeah, lots. Maya in Seattle, like I said, best friend since fifth grade. My CWU group — there's Priya, Jordan, and Sam, we all did the comm associate's together and we hang out at least twice a week, usually at Iron Horse Brewery or someone's apartment. Then there's my hiking people from the Seattle Hiking Collective — Brooke especially, she's like thirty but she's a friend, we go up to Snow Lake or wherever every couple of weekends. Linda Tang from the festival, she's more of a mentor but also a friend. And my volleyball league at the community center, there's like six of us who actually hang out after games. Romantic partners — I had a boyfriend, Tyler, sophomore through senior year of high school, but we broke up last June. He's at WSU. We're, like, civil, not friends.

follow_ups.question: What broke you and Tyler up?
follow_ups.response: He wanted to do the long-distance thing super seriously and I was like, I'm eighteen, I don't want to schedule FaceTimes for the next four years. Also he never wanted to do anything spontaneous. Boring, kind of.

follow_ups.question: How did you meet Brooke from the hiking collective?
follow_ups.response: REI hosted this meetup back in like August 2024, like a beginner trail run-thing, and we ended up at the back of the pack together because we both kept stopping to take pictures. She's a graphic designer in Bellevue, so we've actually talked about her hiring me for some freelance stuff.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: So we live in a little neighborhood on the west side of Ellensburg, off Manitoba Avenue, in a single-family home my parents bought in 2011. It's a pretty quiet area, lots of families, lots of CWU faculty, kind of a mix. There's a park at the end of the block, Mountain View Park, where I walk Mochi every morning. Downtown Ellensburg is like a ten-minute drive, with all the cute coffee shops on Pearl Street — D&M Coffee is my favorite, that's where I do most of my homework. Ellensburg is small, like twenty thousand people not counting students, and it's surrounded by farmland and rolling hills and the Cascades are visible. Winters are cold and windy — Ellensburg is famously windy, it's a joke — and summers are hot and dry. I like it but it's small. I've been here my whole life.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go when you need to get out of Ellensburg?
follow_ups.response: Seattle, mostly, like once or twice a month. I drive my mom's Subaru over Snoqualmie Pass. Sometimes Yakima for the farmers market or Leavenworth for the Bavarian thing. Once a year my friends and I do a Portland trip.

follow_ups.question: Is your neighborhood diverse?
follow_ups.response: Not super. It's mostly white. There's a few other Asian families, some Mexican-American families, but yeah, it's pretty white. CWU brings more diversity into town but the residential parts are pretty homogeneous.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Super safe. I walk Mochi at like 6:30 AM and at 10 PM and I've never felt nervous. My parents don't even lock the back door half the time, which drives my mom's mom crazy when she visits. The only time I felt weird was when somebody egged our mailbox in 2020 during, you know, all that anti-Asian stuff, but that was one time.

follow_ups.question: Did your family talk about that mailbox incident?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, my dad was really upset, more than I'd ever seen him. He cleaned it off himself before I got home from school. We didn't report it, my parents didn't want a fuss.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Up — it's beautiful, it's safe, it's affordable, the outdoor access is unreal. Down — it's small, it's culturally pretty limited, the nearest Asian grocery store is in Yakima or Seattle, and there's no real dating pool. Also, the rodeo is fun but the cowboy aesthetic is, um, not really my vibe.

follow_ups.question: Do you want to leave eventually?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, for sure. Seattle or Portland for a few years at least. Then maybe come back when I'm older.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it's me, my mom Wei, my dad Jianhua, my little brother Andy, and Nai Nai is here through July before she goes back to Chengdu. So five people plus Mochi the dog. Nai Nai sleeps in the guest room which used to be my dad's office. Andy and I have our own rooms upstairs. It's a pretty full house when she's here.

follow_ups.question: How do meals work with everyone there?
follow_ups.response: We mostly eat together at like 6:30 PM on weeknights, my mom or Nai Nai cooks, it's always Chinese food when Nai Nai is around. Weekends are more chaotic, everybody does their own thing.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Nai Nai is sort of temporary — she's here about six months a year. Everybody else is permanent.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that.
transcript.response: Auntie Mei comes down from Vancouver for like a week at Christmas usually. That's it.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everybody who lives here is here right now.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Okay so I just finished my associate's, so right now I'm in this weird in-between phase. Most weekdays I wake up around 8 — or 9 if I forgot to set an alarm, which is often — walk Mochi, eat whatever Nai Nai's making for breakfast, usually congee or steamed buns. Then I do volunteer stuff for the upcoming Lunar New Year fall mini-festival, I'm on the comms team. That's two-three hours of Canva, posting on the Instagram, emailing vendors. Tuesday and Thursday afternoons I'm at the community center for volleyball at 6 PM. Wednesdays I usually drive to Seattle to see Maya and do some street photography. Weekends are hiking — Saturday almost always, sometimes Sunday too. I'm also picking up shifts at D&M Coffee starting in June, just a few hours a week for money. Evenings are usually with the CWU friend group or Andy and the K-dramas.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Like 12:30, 1 AM. I'm not a morning person, which is bad because Mochi is.

follow_ups.question: How do you balance all this with not having a 'real' job yet?
follow_ups.response: I'm living at home so my expenses are low, and the volunteer work is building my portfolio for UW. My parents are okay with it as long as I'm making progress, which is fair.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: Right now I'm not really officially employed — I just graduated with my associate's like two weeks ago. I have a coffee shop gig starting in June at D&M Coffee, like ten to fifteen hours a week, mornings mostly. Other than that I'm doing volunteer social media for the Ellensburg Lunar New Year Cultural Society, which is unpaid but they sometimes give me gift cards. I babysit occasionally for a neighbor, the Hendersons, for cash. Over the next year I want to get an actual marketing internship in Seattle, maybe at a small agency, but I haven't landed one yet.

follow_ups.question: What did D&M Coffee hire you for specifically?
follow_ups.response: Barista plus they want me to help with their Instagram, which was the selling point. The owner is named Becky and she's been wanting to do reels but doesn't know how.

follow_ups.question: Have you applied to internships yet?
follow_ups.response: I've sent out like eight applications to Seattle and Portland agencies. One interview at a place called Wexley School for Girls, which is a real agency name I swear, but they passed.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: Um, I'm in charge of walking Mochi morning and night. I'm supposed to do the dishes at home, which I do, eventually. I drive Andy to his orthodontist appointments because my mom works weird shifts. And I help my dad with anything tech-related — setting up his phone, the printer, whatever. Oh, and I do the family group chat — I'm the one who reminds everybody about Nai Nai's medication times when she's here.

follow_ups.question: What medications does Nai Nai take?
follow_ups.response: Blood pressure stuff, and a blood thinner. She's pretty healthy for eighty-two, knock on wood. I just have a phone reminder for 8 AM and 8 PM.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Big change is I just finished my associate's like literally last week, so the school structure of my day is gone. Suddenly I have all this free time and I'm both loving it and also freaking out a little because I don't have a clear next step until UW decisions come in. Also Nai Nai arrived in April, which always shifts the household rhythm — more cooking, more Mandarin spoken in the house, less freedom for Andy to play video games loudly.

follow_ups.question: When do UW decisions come back?
follow_ups.response: I think early August for transfer. I'm checking the portal probably every day, which is unhealthy.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Oh, I don't have kids. I'm eighteen. Hard pass for now.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Honestly, almost none. I got pulled over once last summer for a busted taillight on Canyon Road and the officer was super chill, just gave me a fix-it ticket. That's it for me personally. Ellensburg PD has been around at festivals I've worked, like for crowd control, and they've always been fine, friendly even.

follow_ups.question: Was the officer who pulled you over someone you knew?
follow_ups.response: No, but it's a small town, my dad knew his name later. Officer Ramirez or something.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Not really. I mean, growing up my parents were always a little tense around cops because they're immigrants and you just internalize that, but I've never had a bad experience.

follow_ups.question: Did your parents talk about that with you?
follow_ups.response: Not directly. It was more like, 'always be polite, hands on the wheel, don't argue.' Standard immigrant-kid talk.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No, nobody in my immediate family or close friend group has ever been arrested as far as I know. One kid from my high school got a DUI but he wasn't really a friend.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I just turned eighteen in February, so I haven't voted in a real election yet, but I'm registered and I'm planning to vote in every one going forward. I voted in a school board recall thing in March 2026, that was my first ballot, which was kind of anticlimactic — just a piece of paper at the kitchen table. I want to vote in the midterms this fall obviously.

follow_ups.question: How did you decide on the school board recall?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, my mom and I talked about it. She's connected to the schools through her nursing work and she had strong opinions. I researched a little and basically agreed with her.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd describe myself as a progressive Democrat, I guess. I care a lot about climate, that's huge for me — living in the PNW you see fire season getting worse every year, and the forests are something I love personally. I'm pro-choice, pro-LGBTQ rights, pro-immigration obviously because I'm a child of immigrants. I think the cost of college is insane and I support free or much cheaper community college and four-year. I'm pro-union, I think. I'm not super radical though — like I have friends who are full DSA socialist and I don't quite get there. I think markets can work, just with way more regulation. I'm not anti-gun in a blanket way because half my friends here hunt, but I think we need way better gun laws. On foreign policy I'm pretty soft, I don't know enough. On China specifically I'm conflicted because, like, the Chinese government does terrible stuff, but the way American media talks about Chinese people sometimes is gross. Overall I'd say center-left, urban Pacific Northwest progressive, but I'm 18 so I reserve the right to change my mind a lot.

follow_ups.question: Where do your political views come from — family, friends, internet?
follow_ups.response: A mix. My parents are moderate Democrats, like they vote D but they're pretty fiscally conservative immigrant-style. My friends pushed me leftward, especially Priya, she's the most political person I know. And TikTok, honestly, like more than I want to admit.

follow_ups.question: Is there a politician or commentator you actually pay attention to?
follow_ups.response: I like Pramila Jayapal because she's local and Indian-American immigrant and a woman, the trifecta. I watch Hasan Piker sometimes, which feels embarrassing to admit. And John Oliver, even though he's a comedian, but he explains stuff clearly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I've gotten more progressive in the last two years, definitely. In high school I was kind of a moderate I-don't-care person, like politics was for grown-ups. Then COVID and the anti-Asian hate stuff happened, and then I started really paying attention. Doing the festival work and meeting more people, including queer folks and refugees, has made me a lot more empathetic on those issues than I was at fifteen. Also climate, like I said — the smoke in summer 2023 and 2024 was really radicalizing in a quiet way.

follow_ups.question: Is there an issue where you've moved rightward at all?
follow_ups.response: Hmm. Maybe on, like, public safety in cities? I was hardcore defund-the-police in 2020 because I was fifteen and that was the vibe online. Now I'm more like, we need better-trained police AND social workers, not no police. So that's probably more centrist than I used to be.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat a lot, I'd say. As an Asian American it hit differently — I obviously support BLM, and the anti-Asian hate wave that happened around the same time made me feel like, you know, all our experiences with American racism are connected, even if they're different. I went to a small BLM march in Ellensburg in 2020, it was like fifty people, which was actually a lot for here. And I've been part of conversations with my parents about why we should be in solidarity with Black communities, which my parents weren't super on board with at first, honestly.

follow_ups.question: What was the conversation with your parents like?
follow_ups.response: Hard. My dad has some — like, model-minority assumptions about Black Americans that I've been pushing back on for years. We're better than we used to be but it's slow.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core thing — that Black Americans deserve to be safe from state violence — is just true and important. The bigger structural questions about how to fix policing are harder. I don't know the answer. I think defunding-and-redirecting to social services makes sense for a lot of stuff, but I also think there's real violent crime that needs a real response. I try to listen to Black voices on this more than I talk, because it's not my experience.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: It's exhausting, honestly. There's the Asian-American conversation that's growing, which I'm part of. There's the Black-white binary that still dominates a lot of the discourse. There's the Latino conversation, the immigration stuff. I think the country is way more multiracial than the conversation usually allows, and I want to see more cross-coalition stuff. I also think a lot of Asian Americans, including older ones in my own family, need to come to terms with being people of color in solidarity with other POC, not adjacent to whiteness.

follow_ups.question: Have you experienced racism yourself?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, the usual stuff. Ching-chong noises in elementary school, the 'where are you really from' thing, COVID-era 'kung flu' jokes from one kid in high school. Nothing that traumatized me but enough that I know what it is.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: All of the above. I've talked to my family, sometimes argued with them. I went to the BLM march in 2020. I've posted on Instagram. I've done some volunteer work with a multicultural student group at CWU. I haven't done anything super heavy though.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friend group is pretty engaged. Priya goes to protests in Seattle. Maya is in nursing school and talks about racial disparities in health all the time. Jordan is more centrist and we argue, but in a friendly way. My parents are kind of avoidant on it, they don't want to be 'political'. My dad came around more after the anti-Asian stuff because it hit close to home.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: I'm healthy, I'd say very healthy. I hike a lot, I play volleyball, I'm 18 and my joints work. I have mild asthma — exercise-induced, I have an albuterol inhaler that I use maybe once a month. I have seasonal allergies in the spring, like right now, and I take Zyrtec. Other than that, no chronic stuff, no surgeries, no broken bones. My eyesight is okay, I have reading glasses but I forget to wear them.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, Dr. Patel at Kittitas Valley Family Medicine. I've been seeing her since I was like ten. My mom works in the same hospital system so I'm pretty covered.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy — I live somewhere with trails everywhere, I have an active friend group, my mom cooks healthy mostly, and I have good insurance through her. Hard — I don't sleep enough, like really not enough, I'm a night owl, and I forget to drink water, and I almost never stretch or cool down after exercise so my hamstrings are wrecked.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever pulled something from skipping cool-downs?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, I tweaked my IT band on a hike last October. Took like three weeks to feel normal. I still didn't really learn my lesson.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The IT band thing last fall was the biggest one. Other than that, my asthma was confirmed as exercise-induced by Dr. Patel in like late 2024, which wasn't a surprise but it was a formal diagnosis. I had COVID once in 2023, mild case, lost smell for like a week. That's about it.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Not really for me personally. The IT band thing kept me from volleyball for a few weeks, that was annoying.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yeah, my Nai Nai's blood pressure stuff has been on my mind. She had a small stroke in 2022 in China, before I really knew, and she came to live with us for longer stretches after that. I'm one of the people who watches her medication schedule and makes sure she doesn't skip walks. My grandpa in Hangzhou has dementia that's getting worse and my mom is really stressed about that — she's been trying to figure out if she should go back for a longer visit.

follow_ups.question: Is your mom planning to go to China?
follow_ups.response: We're not sure. She's talking about taking three weeks in November. That would be a lot for our family.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have it good. My mom works at the hospital so we have employer health insurance through Kittitas Valley Healthcare, and she knows the system inside and out. We've never had to skip care that I know of. Dental is a little more annoying — there's only like two dentists in town who take our plan, and the wait list is long. But medical is fine.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Oh definitely. Nai Nai is all-in on traditional Chinese medicine — she drinks bitter herb teas, she does cupping when her shoulder hurts, she went to an acupuncturist in Yakima a few times last year. My mom is the bridge — she's a Western-trained nurse but she also believes in some of the traditional stuff. I'm somewhere in the middle — I've done acupuncture for stress, I drink the herbal teas when Nai Nai makes them, but I trust Western medicine for anything serious.

follow_ups.question: What did the acupuncture feel like?
follow_ups.response: Honestly relaxing. The needles don't hurt, you just kind of lie there. I'd do it again.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I'm under 21 so I'm not supposed to drink, but, I mean, I've had some at parties. Mostly beer at like Iron Horse or wine if my mom's pouring at dinner. I don't smoke anything regularly. I tried weed gummies at a friend's place once in March, didn't love it, made me anxious. I don't really use substances to cope, I'd rather hike or eat my feelings honestly.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: Nope, no prescription stuff except the inhaler and Zyrtec. No pain meds beyond like ibuprofen for cramps. My most recent substance experience was that weed gummy I just mentioned, like two months ago, and I don't think I'll do that again, at least not until I'm in a setting where I feel chill about it.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Through my mom's insurance, like I said. It's good coverage, hospital employee plan. I'm on her plan as a dependent. Andy too. Nai Nai is on Medicare plus traveler's insurance from China when she comes. We're not stressed about paying for healthcare, which I know is a huge privilege.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I'm fully on the vaccine train. Got my COVID shots, the bivalent, the flu shot every year because my mom forces me to. I'll get whatever the CDC recommends.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My mom, first of all, because she's a nurse. The CDC website. NPR. My doctor Dr. Patel. I don't trust random TikTok for medical stuff, even though I'll watch a TikTok about anything else.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Mostly really good, honestly. I finished the associate's, which was a milestone, I have great friends, I'm doing creative work I love. There've been some lows — the Tyler breakup last June was sad for like a month, and the UW waiting-for-decisions thing is making me anxious. I had a stretch in February-March where I felt kind of stuck and uninspired, kind of like a quarter-life crisis at 18, which is ridiculous. But overall my year has been good. I'm an optimistic person by nature, I think.

follow_ups.question: What pulled you out of the February-March slump?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, planning a backpacking trip with Brooke to Olympic National Park in April. Having something to look forward to that was outdoors and with a friend reset me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Yeah, so right after Tyler and I broke up in June 2025, I was a mess for like three weeks. I'd been with him almost three years, and even though I knew the breakup was right, it was lonely. I'd cry at random times, I lost interest in stuff, I didn't want to go hiking. My mom noticed and made me my favorite — beef noodle soup — without asking. Maya drove out from Seattle to spend a weekend with me. Slowly I came out of it, and I felt more myself by late July. It also helped that I started shooting a wedding for a family friend that month and that gave me purpose.

follow_ups.question: Did you reach out for help or wait for people to notice?
follow_ups.response: Maya I texted. My mom noticed on her own. I don't always know how to ask for help, I'm working on that.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I think I have some anxiety, low-key, especially about the future and big decisions. I haven't been formally diagnosed, I haven't seen a therapist. I'm thinking about it actually — CWU has free counseling and I might use it before I lose access. I don't think I'm depressed, I just have periods where I worry too much.

follow_ups.question: What does the anxiety feel like when it's bad?
follow_ups.response: Tight chest, racing thoughts, can't sleep, replaying conversations from like three years ago. Standard stuff I guess.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: My mom is anxious chronically, I think she'd say. She masks it well but I see it. My dad is steady, very even. Andy is starting puberty so he's all over the place emotionally. Nai Nai is the chillest person in the house.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Religion, not really. I'm not religious. My family isn't either, technically — my dad's side is loosely Buddhist, like cultural Buddhist, my mom's side is also vaguely Buddhist, but nobody goes to temple or anything. We do the ancestor stuff at Qingming — like, sweep the family graves metaphorically since they're in China, we light some incense at home. Spirituality, I'd say a little. I have moments on mountains where I feel something that I'd call spiritual. Sunsets too. I don't have a name for it. I don't pray. I don't believe in a personal god. I respect people who do, though.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about death, an afterlife, with family?
follow_ups.response: Not really. When Nai Nai's husband — my Yeh Yeh — died in 2018, we talked about it a little. Nai Nai believes he's around, in some sense. My parents are agnostic about it. I'm agnostic too.

follow_ups.question: Would you raise kids with religion someday?
follow_ups.response: Probably not formal religion, but I'd want them to know about Chinese spiritual traditions and to be respectful of other religions. Maybe meditation, that kind of stuff.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I'm on a lot of them. Instagram is my main one — I post photography there, mostly festival shots, hike pictures, sometimes food. I have like 1,200 followers, mostly people I know. TikTok I scroll way too much, I post very occasionally, mostly stuff I make in Capcut. Snapchat just with close friends, mostly Maya. Discord for the CWU group and my cousin Kevin. I do not use Facebook except for Marketplace and one Chinese-American student group. Twitter I deleted in like 2023. I have a LinkedIn that's barely populated. WeChat for relatives in China, basically forced.

follow_ups.question: How much time would you guess you're on social media a day?
follow_ups.response: Honestly? Like four hours probably. I should cut it down. My screen time report makes me want to cry.

follow_ups.question: Does your photography Instagram have a separate handle?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, it's like @qiao.captures or something dumb I named when I was sixteen. I'm going to rebrand it.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: Not financial, ever. Emotional, kind of — I'll DM Maya or post a vague-sad story sometimes, and people will check in. I wouldn't post like a full breakdown publicly, that's not my style.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress is up a little because of UW applications and the uncertainty. Coping is — more hiking, more cooking, talking to Maya, journaling sometimes. I've been trying meditation through the Calm app, which I'm bad at but trying.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: My mom Wei, my dad Jianhua, my brother Andy, and my grandma Nai Nai who's here through July. And Mochi the dog.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everybody's here.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: My parents, my mom and dad. The mortgage is theirs.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: For me personally — gas for the Subaru, that's like $140 a month with my Seattle trips. My phone bill, which my dad pays but I owe him $35 a month. Eating out with friends, probably $200. A new camera lens I impulse-bought, $300 used. For the household, my parents handle mortgage, groceries, utilities, all that.

follow_ups.question: What lens did you buy?
follow_ups.response: A Sigma 35mm 1.4 for the Canon. Used on KEH. It's lovely. I shouldn't have bought it but I'm not sorry.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: I don't know the household total — that's parent territory. I'd guess our mortgage is like $1,800 and groceries another $900-ish because Nai Nai cooks Chinese which means lots of fresh produce and meat. Utilities, insurance, all that. Maybe $4,500 a month total? I don't really know.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: We own. My parents bought in 2011, it's a three-bedroom ranch on the west side.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Heating is a big winter spike — Ellensburg winters are no joke, our gas bill probably triples December through February. AC bumps up the electric in July and August. Lunar New Year my parents go all out on food and red envelopes for relatives, so January is expensive. My CWU tuition was a chunk in fall and spring semesters. The big variable expense was honestly my mom's flights to Vancouver to see Auntie Mei a few times.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: My parents handle most of it — they have savings. For my personal stuff, I babysit, I had some graduation money, and I sometimes sell prints of my photos at the Saturday market for a few bucks.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: I have a savings account at BECU that my parents opened for me when I was little. I have like $2,100 in it from a combination of red envelope money over the years, babysitting, and a high school job at the Yakima River Trading Co. I also have a Roth IRA my dad made me open last year with $500 in it, because he's like that. I don't save super systematically but I try not to spend everything.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: I'm saving for the move to Seattle if I get into UW — first month's rent, deposit, all that. And for a future Kyoto trip, which is more dream than plan right now.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: No debt. My parents paid for the associate's, which I'm grateful for and aware not everyone has. If I go to UW I'll probably have some loans, depending on scholarships. I have one credit card, a Discover student card, that I pay off every month, mostly to build credit.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: Needed, no. Wanted, sure — there's a Mitski concert in Vancouver in October that I really want to go to and I'm not sure I can swing the ticket plus travel. But that's a want.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Right now I'd say I'm a student transitioning into the workforce — not employed yet officially. The closest thing to an occupation is my volunteer comms work for the Ellensburg Lunar New Year Cultural Society, where I do social media management, flyer design in Canva, event photography, and coordinating with vendors. Activities include drafting posts in English and Mandarin, designing flyers and Instagram graphics, shooting events, editing photos in Lightroom, responding to DMs from the community, and meeting weekly with Linda and the planning committee.

follow_ups.question: How many hours a week is that volunteer role?
follow_ups.response: Like ten on a slow week, twenty when we're close to an event. Right now it's medium because we're three months out from the fall festival.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No, it's volunteer.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: Paid work — I did babysitting and occasional photography gigs, so maybe twenty weeks total in the past year, if you count weeks where I worked at all.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: Three to six paid hours a week, on average.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: Yeah, I babysat for the Hendersons on Saturday for four hours. $80.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Babysitting and the occasional photo gig — those are sort of two things. The coffee shop hasn't started yet.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Two — babysitting, and I shot a senior portrait session for a family friend's kid.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: About $400. $160 from babysitting two times, $240 from the portrait session.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Whenever a gig finishes, basically. Cash or Venmo from the Hendersons, Venmo from photo clients.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: I'm guessing. My mom makes like $85,000 a year as a nurse, my dad maybe $110,000 as an engineer. So combined household income, maybe $16,000 a month gross. I don't really know after taxes.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yeah, I filed for the first time this year, for 2025 income. My dad walked me through TurboTax. I had like $3,200 in earned income and got a small refund.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job?
transcript.response: No real job, so no real benefits. The volunteer gig gives me free festival merch and gift cards sometimes.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: Linda is more like a mentor than a boss. The volunteer team is small, like seven of us, and we get along well — mostly women in their 20s and 30s plus some aunties.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Completely flexible because it's volunteer. We have a weekly Zoom on Tuesday nights and otherwise I work when I work. I love the flexibility but I also know a real job won't be like this.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: No kids, not applicable.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No, none of that.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: My income is always low because I'm a student, but I'm not making ends meet on my own — my parents support me. There were months where I made literally zero and that was fine, I just spent less.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: I have it — like I said, I've got $2,100 in BECU. If it was bigger, my parents would help.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Very privileged and pretty anxious about the future at the same time. I know my parents are taking care of me and the household runs smoothly. I also know that the moment I'm on my own — Seattle rent is brutal, internships are unpaid, the path I want isn't lucrative right away. I worry about not being a financial burden. I want to learn to be self-sufficient.

transcript.response: Never married. Not living with a romantic partner. Single.

transcript.response: February 14, 2008. Yes, Valentine's Day, please don't say anything.

transcript.response: Born in the U.S. — Ellensburg, Washington.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: Ellensburg, Washington. Same place I live now.

transcript.response: No.

transcript.response: Asian — specifically Chinese American.

transcript.response: No.

transcript.response: None, really. Culturally Buddhist-adjacent from my family, but I'd call myself non-religious or agnostic.

transcript.response: Democrat. Pretty strongly, I'd say. Not super partisan, but I can't see myself voting Republican any time soon given where the GOP is right now.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Democratic Party, for sure.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Ellensburg, Washington. Same place. I've never lived anywhere else.

transcript.response: Yes, both.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: My brother Andy, and Nai Nai when she was visiting.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: Master's degree — Master of Science in Electrical Engineering from the University of Washington.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: Bachelor's in Nursing — BSN. From a Chinese university originally, then re-credentialed here.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, she's worked the whole time.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Registered nurse. She works at Kittitas Valley Healthcare on the med-surg floor mostly. Her duties — medication administration, patient assessments, charting, coordinating with doctors, family communication, twelve-hour shifts.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: A community hospital — Kittitas Valley Healthcare. It serves the whole rural area around here, plus the CWU students. It's not huge but it's the main hospital in the county.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Electrical engineer at Bonneville Power Administration. He works on substation maintenance and power grid planning. Lots of CAD, lots of meetings, occasional field visits to substations.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: Bonneville Power Administration — it's a federal agency under the Department of Energy. They manage the high-voltage power grid across the Pacific Northwest, including a lot of hydroelectric from the Columbia River dams.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: In three to five years, I want to be living in Seattle or Portland with a bachelor's in communications or marketing, working at a small agency or in-house at a culturally diverse org — maybe a museum, maybe a nonprofit, maybe a brand I actually care about. I want my own place with one roommate and a dog. I want to be visiting my parents often but on my own terms. I want to be dating someone who challenges me. I want to have traveled to Japan and maybe back to China to see my mom's family. Long-term I want to start my own little boutique event-planning and marketing consultancy focused on multicultural community events, especially Asian American festivals. I want to be financially stable enough that my parents don't worry. And I want to still be hiking and making art and laughing a lot.

follow_ups.question: What kind of dog?
follow_ups.response: A corgi like Mochi, or a shiba inu. Something small and dramatic.

follow_ups.question: What does 'someone who challenges you' mean?
follow_ups.response: Like, someone who pushes me to be braver, more disciplined, more honest. Not someone who fights with me, but someone with their own thing going on, who has opinions, who reads.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Family, probably first. My parents sacrificed a lot to come here and give me this life and I feel that. Then my friendships — they're like a second family. Creativity, like having space to make stuff and express. Connection across cultures. The outdoors, mountains specifically. And being kind. I really think being kind is underrated.

follow_ups.question: If you had to pick one of those as the most important?
follow_ups.response: Family. With friendships a really close second.
